title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
hook: the streetlights come on and, in some homes, a small lamp too: the day has joints, and the routine marks them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine, dinacharya, reached past the skin: sadvritta, good conduct, and the advice to greet first, with a friendly face. Who did you speak to first? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

Dusk, and the streetlights blink on one after another down the block. In some Hindu homes, around the same moment, someone lights a small lamp in front of the family shrine. Nobody announces it. The light outside is changing, so the light inside is changed too. Day turning into night is one of the day's joints, the places where one part bends into the next. Dawn is another. Hindu practice has paid attention to those joints for a long time, and so does the daily round. On our last day with it: the joints of the day, and what to do when life bends the routine.
screen: `STREETLIGHTS, AND A SMALL LAMP.` → `THE DAY HAS JOINTS.` → `WHEN LIFE BENDS THE ROUTINE.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is sandhya: a joining, a twilight, the meeting point of two parts of the day. Some Hindus keep prayers at these meeting points, called sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, at dawn and at dusk, and for some at noon too. Lamps lit at dusk come from the same attention. The Ayurvedic texts notice the joints from another side. Among their rules of good conduct, paraphrased, the Charaka Samhita advises against eating, sleeping or studying at the twilights. Whatever the reasons a reader finds there, the effect is the same: the joints of the day are kept a little apart, a little quieter. So the daily round, which began before sunrise, has shape all day: a waking, the senses, the oil, effort in measure, kind speech, and pauses at the turns. Now the honest part. Plenty of lives don't fit a dawn-to-dusk shape. Night shifts. A newborn. Illness. A job that starts at four. Does the routine just break? Read closely, the texts already leave room. The verse about waking addressed the healthy person. Exercise was measured to strength and season. And in the Ashtanga Hridaya, the chapter after the day is the year: how the routine changes with the seasons. A routine that changes with the year isn't a rigid one. So when life bends the schedule, the round doesn't have to be thrown out. Keep the pieces that fit. Mark the joints you actually have: waking, a meal, the end of a shift. Turn each into a small pause. The routine follows the person, the way the texts follow the season.
screen: `SANDHYA: THE DAY'S JOINTS` · `KEEP THE JOINTS A LITTLE QUIET` · `PLENTY OF LIVES DON'T FIT` · `THE ROUTINE FOLLOWS THE PERSON`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your own joints. Close the eyes if that's comfortable. Walk through a usual day, yours, not an ideal one. Where does one part bend into the next? Waking. Leaving the house. A meal. Coming home. The last light switched off. Choose one of those joints. See yourself pausing there for a single breath, before going on. Rest in this breath now, as if this moment were a joint too. If you pray, you can let a prayer you already know mark that joint. The bell holds the time.
The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct, from waking to the twilight, built to bend to the person who keeps it. Today's word.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. Today, at one joint of your actual day, a door, a meal, a switch flicked off, stop for one breath before going on. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

notes: Last of seven dinacharya days; tomorrow begins the seasons (ritucharya).

Charaka Sutrasthana 8 twilight rule (not eating, sleeping, studying, or sexual activity at the sandhyas) recalled from memory; confirm verse and list. The script names only eating, sleeping and studying.

Sandhyavandana: the script says 'some Hindus', 'at dawn and at dusk, and for some at noon too'. Traditionally associated with those who have had the sacred-thread ceremony; the script does not go into who is obliged. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this framing.
'Lamps lit at dusk come from the same attention': confirm this link between the evening lamp and sandhya is acceptable.
'Hindu practice has paid attention to those joints for a long time' avoids any date; confirm.
